assessment.nobel_worthiness: A new topological classification of electronic states, protected by time-reversal symmetry, predicted by theory and realised in real materials. It is a clear case of the kind of discovery I value: a genuinely new quantum state of matter, quantitatively explained by band-structure theory and tied to measured transport and spectroscopy. It reshaped condensed-matter physics and opened the broader field of topological materials.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the decisive theoretical step (the Z2 invariant and the quantum spin Hall proposal in graphene). Molenkamp's group gave the first experimental demonstration in HgTe/CdTe quantum wells, following the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang prediction, which is not in the supplied credit list. That omission is a fairness concern, but the three credited names form a coherent theory-plus-experiment trio.
assessment.maturity: Roughly twenty years since the key papers, with many independent confirmations across HgTe, InAs/GaSb, Bi-based compounds and ARPES studies of 3D topological insulators. The interpretation is stable and the field is mature, so recognition is timely and not premature.
uncertainties: Whether the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang prediction, or the 3D topological insulator work (Fu, Kane, Mele; Moore and Balents; Hsieh and Hasan), should share credit; the supplied names cannot cover all of them.
Whether the committee would prefer to define the prize around the broader topological-insulator concept and not around the 2D quantum spin Hall case.
I am relying on my own recollection of the history and have not verified it independently.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Theory predicted flat moire bands at a magic angle in twisted bilayer graphene. Experiment then found correlated insulators and superconductivity in the same system. It is a new tunable platform for strongly correlated physics, and it surprised the community. The link between a calculable band-structure prediction and a measured phase diagram is the sort of result I find convincing.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald made the continuum-model prediction of the magic angle, and Jarillo-Herrero's group made the 2018 experimental discoveries (with Cao and others, not credited here). Pablo Jarillo-Herrero is the clear experimental lead. Credit to the first-author experimentalist Yuan Cao and to Allan MacDonald's collaborators is a possible complication, and the three-name limit is tight.
assessment.maturity: Since 2018 there has been rapid independent confirmation by many groups, and the field is now very large. The microscopic origin of the superconductivity and of the correlated phases is still debated. The discovery of the effect is solid, but a full explanation is not yet available, so the timing is somewhat early.
uncertainties: The mechanism of superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene remains unresolved.

Credit for the 2018 experiments extends beyond Jarillo-Herrero (for example Yuan Cao), and the early moire-band theory had other contributors (for example Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto), who are not credited here.
Sample-dependence and twist-angle disorder complicate reproducibility.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cold atoms in optical lattices realise Hubbard-type models with tunable parameters, and they observed the superfluid to Mott-insulator transition and, later, fermionic correlations and single-site resolved imaging. This is a deep link between condensed-matter theory and a controllable experiment, and it gives quantitative tests of many-body theory. The impact on quantum simulation is large.
assessment.attribution: The Mott-insulator experiment (Greiner, Mandel, Hansch, Bloch) and the later fermionic Hubbard work (Esslinger) are decisive, while the theoretical proposal (Jaksch, Zoller and others) is a separate strand. Cirac and Zoller are credited in this entry but I would reserve their recognition for the theory-focused entry, so I choose the three experimentalists. A five-name credit list shows how crowded the attribution is.
assessment.maturity: More than twenty years of work, with many independent groups reproducing and extending it. The interpretation is stable and the field is mature.
uncertainties: Credit for the foundational theory (the Jaksch et al. proposal) is not fully covered by the names supplied.
The scope is broad, so the prize definition could overlap with the separate quantum-computation-theory candidate and with the 2012 and 2001 AMO prizes.
Quantitative demonstrations of useful quantum advantage in simulation remain open.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength optical lattice clock, and the technique has taken clock precision to the 10^-18 level. That is a spectacular quantitative achievement, with applications in tests of fundamental physics, relativistic geodesy and a possible redefinition of the second. The discovery is clear and the experimental results are reproducible across laboratories.
assessment.attribution: Katori is the originator of the lattice-clock concept, and Jun Ye's group made the leading precision demonstrations and many-body clock advances. Both names are credited, a two-person prize is natural, and the contributions are well separated. Other groups (for example the NIST and JILA colleagues, and the groups around Lemonde and Takamoto) also made important contributions.
assessment.maturity: Independent confirmation by several national laboratories, and the technique is mature. The 2005 prize recognised the frequency comb, which sits close by, so there may be some perception of overlap, but this concept is distinct.
uncertainties: Whether the committee sees this as engineering-level metrology or a fundamental physics discovery.
Possible overlap with the earlier Hall and Hansch recognition and with ion-clock work (for example Wineland, 2012).
Which other groups should share credit is not settled by the supplied names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum anomalous Hall effect is a quantised Hall conductance without an external magnetic field, realised in magnetic topological insulators. It is a beautiful realisation of a topological phase tied to magnetism and band structure, which is close to my own field. It has relevance for dissipationless edge transport and for metrology.
assessment.attribution: Fang, Dai and collaborators made the theoretical prediction in Cr- or Fe-doped Bi2Se3-family materials, and Xue's group made the experimental observation in Cr-doped (Bi,Sb)2Te3 films in 2013. Haldane's earlier model, and other contributors such as Chang, Zhang and Qi, are not in the credited names, so the allocation is somewhat uncertain. The experimentalist and theorists listed would nonetheless make a defensible trio.
assessment.maturity: Independently confirmed in several laboratories, though the quantisation temperatures remain low, at about the tens-of-millikelvin scale in most samples. The physics is understood, but the theory-to-experiment history is still contested and recognition might be somewhat early compared with older candidates.
uncertainties: Haldane's 1988 model is a precursor, and the 2016 prize recognised him for topological phases already.
The priority and credit among Chinese and US-based theory and experiment groups is unclear from the supplied names.
The low operating temperature and sample disorder limit practical impact so far.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The discovery of superconductivity in the Bechgaard salts was the first superconductivity in an organic conductor, in a quasi-one-dimensional system with a rich phase diagram of spin-density-wave and superconducting phases near a quantum critical region. It opened up the study of unconventional superconductivity and correlated low-dimensional electrons, and it is a clear new-quantum-behaviour-in-materials story.
assessment.attribution: Bechgaard synthesised the materials and Jerome led the physics discovery with collaborators in 1980. The two credited names are a natural pair, although the original paper had other co-authors (Mazaud, Ribault, Bechgaard), so credit is not fully clean.
assessment.maturity: More than forty years of confirmation and follow-up, with a stable interpretation, although the pairing symmetry remains debated. This is very mature, perhaps even overdue, and there is a risk that principals are no longer all available.
uncertainties: The pairing symmetry and mechanism of superconductivity in these salts are still debated.
Whether the discovery is judged to have had lasting impact comparable to the cuprates and the iron-based materials.
The age of the discovery raises questions about the availability and health of the principals, which I cannot verify.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The discovery of high-temperature superconductivity in iron pnictides and chalcogenides added a second family of high-Tc materials with a different electronic structure, multiband physics and magnetism closely tied to superconductivity. The first-principles electronic structure of these materials is an active area of my own field. It was a surprise, since iron was thought to be harmful to superconductivity.
assessment.attribution: Hosono's group discovered superconductivity in LaFeAsO(1-x)Fx in 2008, and the Chinese groups of Chen and Zhao quickly raised Tc above 50 K with rare-earth substitution. Hosono is clearly the discoverer. Whether the rapid Tc-raising work deserves equal recognition is a question of judgment, so I propose two names and flag the issue.
assessment.maturity: More than fifteen years of independent confirmation, but the pairing mechanism is still unsettled and the maximum Tc has not progressed much beyond about 55 K in bulk. The phenomenon is firmly established, but the lack of a unifying explanation makes the recognition somewhat uncertain.
uncertainties: No consensus on the pairing mechanism.
Division of credit between Hosono and the groups that increased Tc, and whether Chen should be preferred to Zhao.
The cuprate prize in 1987 may make the committee wary of another materials-discovery award without mechanism.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Beaurepaire's 1996 observation of sub-picosecond demagnetization of nickel, and later all-optical magnetic switching by Kimel and Rasing, opened ultrafast magnetism. It is a surprising and technologically suggestive discovery that challenges simple theories of how spin angular momentum can be dissipated so quickly. It is directly in my own area, which I should flag as a source of both knowledge and bias.
assessment.attribution: Beaurepaire made the foundational observation, and Kimel and Rasing demonstrated all-optical switching and its helicity dependence. The two strands are separate (ultrafast demagnetisation versus all-optical switching), and other groups (for example Stohr, Radu and Bigot) also contributed. The three names would need to be framed as one discovery, and that framing is not obvious.
assessment.maturity: The experimental effects are confirmed in many laboratories, but the microscopic mechanisms (spin-orbit-mediated spin flips, superdiffusive transport, exchange-driven transfer) are still debated and my own field has not converged. This places the discovery in a state where the phenomenon is mature but the theory is not, so recognition may be premature.
uncertainties: No consensus on the microscopic mechanism of ultrafast demagnetisation.
A compound discovery whose parts (demagnetisation and all-optical switching) may need different recognition.
As a theorist working on closely related problems, I may overweight this area relative to others.
